study.title: Matthew 14 The rejection, the sustenance and authority of Jesus
study.overview: Matthew 14 presents three great movements: the death of John the Baptist because of the corruption of human power; the miraculous provision of Jesus for the multitude and for the disciples; and the manifestation of his authority over the sea, culminating in the healing of the sick in Genesaré. The chapter contrasts Herod's weakness, the vacillating faith of the disciples, and the powerful compassion of Christ. Throughout the chapter, Jesus appears not only as a prophet or teacher, but as the one who gives bread, rules creation, answers faith and receives worship as the Son of God.

outline.title: Herod, the arrest and death of John the Baptist
outline.explanation: Herod hears of Jesus and interprets miracles as a sign of the risen John. The text then recalls the reason for John's arrest: his direct denunciation of Herod's illicit marriage. The narrative culminates in the banquet, in the precipitated oath, in the manipulation of Herodias and in the execution of the prophet. John's disciples bury the body and warn Jesus, linking the testimony of the forerunner to the Messiah's ministry.

outline.title: Jesus Feeds the crowd in the desert
outline.explanation: Jesus withdraws when he hears the news of John's death, but the crowd follows him. Instead of rejecting them, he has compassion on him, heals the sick and teaches the disciples to share in the provision. With five loaves and two fish, Jesus feeds everyone to satisfaction and still plenty of bread. The signal reveals its ability to meet real human needs, without relying on visible resources.

outline.title: Jesus walks on the sea and strengthens the faith of the disciples
outline.explanation: After dismissing the crowd, Jesus will pray alone, while the disciples face the opposite wind in the sea. At the moment of greater danger, he has been walking on the waters and encourages them: "I am." Peter asks to meet him, but sinks when he looks at the wind and not Jesus. Christ holds him, corrects his little faith and calms the wind; then the disciples worship him and confess his divine identity.

outline.title: Curas in Genesaré
outline.explanation: Upon reaching the other side, Jesus is recognized immediately. The population takes the sick and asks only to touch the edge of their clothes. The result is total: all those who touch it are healed. The end of the chapter shows that the power of Jesus reaches both nature and human suffering, and that his presence attracts practical and trusting faith.

study.context: The chapter is set under Herod's rule, called tetrarch, that is, ruler of a part of the kingdom. The account begins at Herod's court and ends in Genesaré, showing the contrast between the political center marked by guilt and violence, and the places where the presence of Jesus brings life and healing. The mention of John's disciples and the reaction of the multitudes shows that Jesus is already widely known, but also misunderstood by some. The text preserves the memory of John's ministry as a forerunner and shifts the focus to the identity and work of Christ.
study.theology: Matthew 14 teaches that the power of God is not limited by human rejection, material scarcity or forces of nature. John's death shows the cost of faithful witness and the perversity of a power without repentance. The multiplication of the loaves shows Jesus as a compassionate provider, able to supply what the disciples cannot produce. Walking on the sea reveals its sovereignty over creation and also teaches that true faith looks at Christ and not to the wind. The final confession is that he is the Son of God - is the theological climax of the chapter. At the same time, healing in Genesaré shows that the grace of Jesus reaches those who approach him with need and trust. In evangelical reading, the chapter unites compassion, authority, messianic identity and called to faith.

scholarViews.insight: Herod Antipas is presented as the tetrarch, that is, ruler of a part of the kingdom; the note also links his fame to the attempt to explain the miracles of Jesus as if John had risen.
The commentator points out that Jesus sympathized with the crowd, and understands this compassion as a deep tenderness in the face of the misery of others.
The note emphasizes that touching the edge of Jesus" clothing manifests the power and grace of Christ, producing healing in those approaching him.

questions: What does Herod's reaction reveal about a guilty conscience that does not repent?
In which areas do I look more like the disciples, looking at scarcity or to the wind instead of looking at Jesus?
How can I, in a practical way, approach Christ today with the same confidence that the crowd sought to touch his clothes?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader three concrete answers: to speak the truth with fidelity, even when it costs; to trust that Jesus supplies real needs, including when resources seem insufficient; and keep his eyes in his midst of the storms, rather than interpreting the circumstance as impossible. He also invites to seek Jesus with perseverance, leading to him our sicknesses, limitations and fear, certain that his compassion remains active.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not explain in detail the meaning of the cure by the edge of clothing or offer additional data on the geography of Genesaré beyond the text itself and the notes. There is also no basis here to state with certainty the identity of Herodias' daughter beyond the assumption commented by Tyndale. Where there are devotional readings of the commentators, they were treated as interpretations, not as indisputable conclusions of the text.
